lead: A Moore machine prints a symbol every time it enters a state. A Mealy machine prints a symbol every time it takes a transition. Both are transducers: they turn an input string over Σ into an output string over Δ, and neither has final states. They matter because many devices must produce output, not just accept or reject: a vending machine returns change, a traffic light changes lamps, a compiler scanner turns characters into tokens. The two models are equally powerful and convert into each other.
prereq: You need: DFA and transition diagrams and δ̂.

sections.h3: Moore machine: print on the state

blocks.text: A Moore machine is a DFA with output attached to states. When the machine enters a state, it prints that state's symbol immediately.
M = (Q, Σ, Δ, δ, λ, q₀)
blocks.where: Q is the finite set of states; Σ is the input alphabet; Δ is the output alphabet; δ: Q × Σ → Q is the transition function; λ: Q → Δ is the output function; q₀ ∈ Q is the start state.

blocks.text: There is no set of final states. Every input string is processed fully and produces an output string. The start state prints before any input symbol is read.

blocks.where: qᵢ is the state after reading the first i input symbols a₁…aₙ, with qᵢ = δ(qᵢ₋₁, aᵢ). The output has n + 1 symbols for an input of n symbols.

blocks.text: That extra first symbol is part of the definition. If a problem wants exactly n output symbols, it usually says to ignore the first printed symbol.

sections.h3: Mealy machine: print on the edge

blocks.text: A Mealy machine is a DFA with output attached to transitions. When the machine reads a symbol and moves, it prints the output written on that edge.
M = (Q, Σ, Δ, δ, λ, q₀),   λ: Q × Σ → Δ
blocks.where: Q, Σ, Δ, δ and q₀ mean the same as for a Moore machine; λ now takes a state and an input symbol and returns the output symbol printed on that transition.

blocks.text: An edge is labelled a / b: read input symbol a, print output symbol b, and go to the next state. There is no output for the start state because no transition has been taken yet.
For an input of n symbols, a Mealy machine prints exactly n symbols. It has no final states either.
Moore to Mealy is direct. Move each state's output onto every transition that enters that state.

blocks.where: λ′ is the Mealy output function; q is the current state; a is the input symbol; δ(q, a) is the next Moore state; λ of that next state is the symbol printed on the transition. This conversion loses the first printed symbol, so the Mealy output equals the Moore output with λ(q₀) removed.

blocks.text: Mealy to Moore needs more states. A Moore state must remember both the old Mealy state and the output printed on entering it.

items: For every Mealy state q and every output symbol x that some transition prints on entering q, make a Moore state (q, x). Its Moore output is x.
Add a Moore transition from (p, r) on input a to (q, x) when the Mealy transition is p on a to q printing x.
Use start state (q₀, c), where c is a chosen initial output, often 0, because no transition entered q₀.

Keep only reachable states. The construction may create more states than the Mealy machine, but the two print the same symbols in the same order once you allow for that leading symbol: Moore output = c followed by the Mealy output.

blocks.text: The two models are equally powerful. A Mealy machine can sometimes use fewer states because the last printed symbol is carried on the edge, not stored in a state.

figure.caption: Both machines read 0101. Mealy prints one symbol per move, 0101; Moore prints on entering each state, so its start state adds an extra leading 0 and it prints 00101.

examples.question: Design a Mealy machine over {0, 1} that prints 1 whenever the last two bits read are 01, and convert it to a Moore machine. Then run both machines on input 0101.
steps: Name the Mealy states S0 and S1. S0 means the last bit is not 0, or no bit has been read. S1 means the last bit was 0. Start at S0.
Mealy transitions: S0 on 0 goes to S1 and prints 0. S0 on 1 stays at S0 and prints 0. S1 on 0 stays at S1 and prints 0. S1 on 1 goes to S0 and prints 1.
Run Mealy on 0101. Start S0. Read 0: S1, print 0. Read 1: S0, print 1. Read 0: S1, print 0. Read 1: S0, print 1. Mealy output is 0101, four symbols.
Convert to Moore. Make A = (S0, 0) with output 0, B = (S1, 0) with output 0, and C = (S0, 1) with output 1.
Moore transitions: A on 0 goes to B, A on 1 goes to A. B on 0 goes to B, B on 1 goes to C. C on 0 goes to B, C on 1 goes to A.
Run Moore on 0101. Start A, print 0. Read 0: B, print 0. Read 1: C, print 1. Read 0: B, print 0. Read 1: C, print 1. Moore output is 00101, five symbols.
examples.answer: The Mealy machine prints 0101 and the Moore machine prints 00101: the same output sequence with one extra leading 0.

traps: A Moore machine prints n + 1 symbols for n input symbols because the start state prints first. A Mealy machine prints n symbols. Do not compare the two output strings position by position without allowing for the leading Moore symbol.
A Mealy machine may need fewer states than a Moore machine for the same job, because the output can sit on an edge instead of in a state. State counts alone do not prove the machines differ in power.
Both machines have no final states. A question asking for final states is testing whether you confuse a transducer with a DFA acceptor.
In a Moore machine, the output belongs to the state being entered, not the state being left. Read the state note after every move.
In Mealy-to-Moore conversion the start state needs a chosen initial output because no transition enters it. Always say what that initial symbol is.

quiz.q: Write the tuple for a Moore machine and state the type of its output function.
quiz.a: M = (Q, Σ, Δ, δ, λ, q₀), with λ: Q → Δ. Q is states, Σ input alphabet, Δ output alphabet, δ transition function, q₀ start state.

quiz.q: How many output symbols does a Mealy machine print for an input of n symbols, and how many does a Moore machine print?
quiz.a: Mealy prints n symbols. Moore prints n + 1 symbols because the start state prints before any input symbol is read.

quiz.q: Why do Moore and Mealy machines have no set of final states?
quiz.a: They are transducers, not acceptors. They do not accept or reject an input; they process every input string and produce an output string.

quiz.q: Give the Moore-to-Mealy conversion formula and explain each symbol.
quiz.a: λ′(q, a) = λ(δ(q, a)). Here q is the current state, a is the input symbol, δ(q, a) is the next Moore state, and λ of that next state is the output printed on the Mealy transition. The Mealy output equals the Moore output with the leading λ(q₀) removed.

quiz.q: A Mealy machine has S0 on 0 → S1 / 0, S0 on 1 → S0 / 0, S1 on 0 → S1 / 0, S1 on 1 → S0 / 1, start S0. Find the output for input 0101.
quiz.a: Start S0. Read 0: S1, output 0. Read 1: S0, output 1. Read 0: S1, output 0. Read 1: S0, output 1. The output is 0101.

quiz.q: A Moore machine has A with output 0, B with output 1. A on 0 goes to B, A on 1 goes to A, B on 0 goes to A, B on 1 goes to B, start A. Find the output for input 0110.
quiz.a: Start A, print 0. Read 0: go to B, print 1 → 01. Read 1: stay at B, print 1 → 011. Read 1: stay at B, print 1 → 0111. Read 0: go to A, print 0 → 01110. Output is 01110.

quiz.q: Explain why a Moore output string is one symbol longer than a Mealy output string for the same input, and how you would compare the two fairly.
quiz.a: Moore prints the start state's output before reading any symbol, so it adds one leading symbol. To compare, either ignore that first Moore symbol or add a chosen initial symbol to the Mealy output before comparing position by position.

quiz.q: A Mealy machine has 3 states and output alphabet {0, 1}. Give an upper bound on the number of states in a Moore conversion and explain why not all need appear.
quiz.a: Each Moore state is a pair (old state, output printed on entering it), so there are at most 3 × 2 = 6 pairs. Only reachable pairs appear; some pairs may never be entered with that output, so the reachable Moore machine can have fewer than 6 states.

beyond: Not for the exam. In hardware, Mealy outputs can change with the input before a clock edge, while Moore outputs settle after the clock; controllers often prefer Moore for safe timing. In software, lexers behave like Mealy scanners because a token is emitted on consuming a character. Search next for finite-state transducer, transducer composition, and lexical analyzer DFA.
